title: Censuses and the Large Numbers
lead: The Bible records several counts of Israel, from the wilderness censuses of Numbers to David's ill-fated count and the Roman census of Luke 2. The very large numbers of the wilderness generation are among the most debated figures in the Bible.

sections.b: Exodus 30:11–16 requires a half-shekel "ransom" from each man counted, "so that no plague will strike them." Numbers holds two censuses of fighting men, one at Sinai (Numbers 1, 603,550 men) and one on the plains of Moab for the new generation (Numbers 26, 601,730), framing the death of the old generation in between. The Levites are counted separately (Numbers 3–4). David's census in 2 Samuel 24 (1 Chronicles 21) brings a plague, and readers have long asked why: pride, distrust, or the missing ransom of Exodus 30. Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 list the returned exiles by families. In Luke 2:1–5 a Roman census brings Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem. Revelation 7:4–8 numbers 144,000 from the tribes of Israel and then sees a crowd no one could count (Revelation 7:9).
sections.refs: Exodus 30:11–16; Numbers 1:1–46; Numbers 26:1–65; 2 Samuel 24:1–25; 1 Chronicles 21:1–30; Ezra 2:1–70; Luke 2:1–5; Revelation 7:4–9

sections.b: Read as written, about 600,000 men of fighting age (Exodus 12:37; Numbers 1:46) imply two to three million people. Many traditional readers accept this. Others read the Hebrew 'elef, "thousand," as "clan" or "military unit" (Judges 6:15; 1 Samuel 10:19): Flinders Petrie (1906), George Mendenhall (1958) and Colin Humphreys (1998) arrived at roughly 5,500 fighting men. Some see symbolism (the Hebrew letters of "sons of Israel" add up to 603) or hyperbole. Most critical scholars treat the figures as an idealized picture, perhaps drawn from later censuses of the kingdom. The problem of the 22,273 firstborn (Numbers 3:43) and the statement that Israel was "the fewest of all the peoples" (Deuteronomy 7:7) feature in the debate.
